title: PRISM: Parallel Residual Iterative Sequence Model
claim: A sequence layer approximates expensive iterative optimization with a parallel residual solver feeding a state-independent scan, keeping both expressivity and speed.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, left layer stack zoomed into right block via dotted arrow
description: Two-part architecture diagram. The left panel shows a standard stacked layer repeated N times: Layer Norm, a yellow PRISM Layer, a residual add, Layer Norm, a blue FFN, and a second residual add, with Input at the bottom and Output at the top. A dotted blue arrow expands the PRISM Layer into the larger right panel, the PRISM Block. In the block, a blue ShortConv proxy at the bottom feeds beige projection boxes (q, v, k, p) and pink triangles (β, α). These feed a pale-yellow 'Solver: In SRAM' region. Inside it, two chained GELU residual-step boxes pass r(2) = r(1) − δ(1) and sum into B_t. An orange Parallel Scan bar at the top holds the S_t update equation and leads to the output projection. The eye goes first to the orange scan bar and the yellow solver.
caption: The PRISM Architecture. The framework resolves the Rank-Parallel trade-off through two mechanisms. Phase 1 (Input-Anchored Proxy): A ShortConv anchor computes a state-free proxy $u_t \approx S_{t-1}k_t$. Learned predictors generate Contextual Gain vectors $p^{(l)}$ (approximating $\phi'(S_{t-1}k_t)$) and Basis Directions $k^{(l)}$ (approximating the multi-step gradient directions)---all from inputs alone. Phase 2 (Rank-$L$ Accumulation): An unrolled residual loop constructs the high-rank injection $B_t = \sum_{l=1}^L \beta_t^{(l)} \boldsymbol{\delta}_t^{(l)} {k_t^{(l)}}^\top$. Each step performs greedy residual subtraction, expanding the update from Rank-1 to Rank-$L$. State Update: The accumulated Rank-$L$ injection is applied to a decoupled linear recurrence whose forgetting operator $A_t$ is state-independent, preserving parallel scan compatibility.
abstract: Generative sequence modeling faces a fundamental tension between the expressivity of Transformers and the efficiency of linear sequence models. Existing efficient architectures are theoretically bounded by shallow, single-step linear updates, while powerful iterative methods like Test-Time Training (TTT) break hardware parallelism due to two dimensions of serial dependency: token-level state reliance and step-level iteration loops. We propose PRISM (Parallel Residual Iterative Sequence Model) to resolve this tension. PRISM explicitly approximates the expressive gate-residual-direction iteration pattern of TTT in a parallelizable form. We employ a Write-Forget Decoupling strategy that isolates non-linearity within the injection operator. To bypass the serial dependency of explicit solvers, PRISM utilizes a two-stage proxy architecture: a short-convolution anchors the initial residual using local history energy, while a learned predictor estimates the refinement updates directly from the input. This design distills structural patterns associated with iterative correction into a parallelizable feedforward operator. Theoretically, we prove that this formulation achieves Rank-$L$ accumulation, structurally expanding the update scheme beyond the single-step Rank-$1$ bottleneck. Empirically, it achieves comparable performance to explicit optimization methods while achieving \textbf{174x higher throughput}. Codes are available in https://github.com/gpr-prism/prism/.
